replying_to: Replying to SHAQ: Incorporating Shapley Value Theory into Multi-Agent Q-Learning
display_title: Official Review of Paper548 by Reviewer mYrf

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to generalize Shapley value in coalitional game theory to Markov convex game (MCG). It formally proves that the generalized Shapley value lies in the $\epsilon^*$-core of MCG with grand coalition, so it can be used as a value factorization method for  global reward game (each agent can maximize its own generalized Shapley value in order to maximize the global value). The paper also proposes Shapley-Q operator and Shapley Q-learning (SHAQ). Experimental results on predator-prey and SMAC benchmark show that SHAQ can achieve good performance overall, while achieving better interpretability than baseline methods.
content.main_review:
- Strengths:
	- The proposed generalized Shapley value has some quite nice theoretical properties. The proposed Shapley-Q operator also seems solid. 
	- Using Shapley value as a value factorization method with better interpretability is very interesting (but I'm not very sure how novel this idea is given existing work [1]).

- Weaknesses:
	- The motivation for proposing generalized Shapley value is not very clear to me. The authors argue that the main motivation for this is although [1] "gave an analytic form of Shapley value ... the effect of policy is neglected so that it is not promising to be within the core (or ε-core)." I don't quite understand this motivation. 
	- I'm not sure how significant the theoretical contributions are compared to the work in [1], especially what the *practical* differences are between these theoretical results.  
	- Empirical results (especially on SMAC) are not strong enough in my opinion. The authors argue that "Many researchers in MARL regard the performance as the only standard to evaluate an algorithm, while we would argue that the interpretability is also significant, especially to the deployment in industry." While I certainly agree that the performance shouldn't be the only standard to evaluate an algorithm, I'd still expect the proposed method to be able to outperform all existing methods by a *significant margin* on at least one or two tasks, since in the two tested domains, I'm not very sure how useful the interpretability really is. 

- Major questions:
	- The authors provide some discussion about the main differences between their work and [1] (at page 6). Algorithmically, it is clear that they propose a new multi-agent value-based method (SHAQ), while [1] proposes a multi-agent actor-critic method (SQDDPG).  But they share the same key idea of using Shapley Q-values. Theoretically, it seems that the main difference is that the authors fixed a problem in [1] and then show that the generalised Shapley value is a solution in the $\epsilon^*$-core of Markov convex game. I might miss some other important theoretical contributions. Can the authors clarify this? Also, what are the practical differences between your theoretical results and the ones in [1]?
	- The predator-prey tasks chosen in the paper are for modelling relative overgeneralization. Why were these type of tasks chosen? Why are SHAQ and VDN better at tackling relative overgeneralization than other baseline methods? Actually, the term "relative overgeneralization" was never even mentioned before the experiment section about predator-prey. I think more discussion should be provided regarding this. 
	- On predator-prey, why is SQDPPG not compared against (I couldn't find it in the appendix either)? Also, the authors mention that "W-QMIX does not perform as well as reported in Rashid et al. (2020). The reason could be its poor robustness to the increased explorations (Rashid et al., 2020) for this environment." How does W-QMIX perform with less exploration, say annealing $\epsilon$ over 10k/50k timesteps instead of 1mil? 
	- If the generalized Shapley value can be thought of as a linear value factorization, I think it might be useful to discuss the limitations some, as I'd assume some tasks might need a non-linear value factorization to solve. 

**Post-rebuttal:**

I thank the authors' for their detailed rebuttal. It helped clarify some questions I had. However, my main concern regarding the significance of their theoretical contributions remains, especially in terms of the practical differences between their theoretical results and the ones in [1]. Therefore, I decided to maintain my score. 

[1] Shapley q-value: A local reward approach to solve global reward games. Wang et al. AAAI 2020.
content.summary_of_the_review: I'm leaning towards rejecting the paper at this stage since I'm not sure how significant the theoretical contributions are compared to some existing work and the empirical results are not strong enough to me. I'm happy to revise my score though if I underestimate the contributions from either aspects.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Response to Reviewer mYrf (1/2)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the detailed and thoughtful comments. We will try our best to address the concerns from the reviewer.

1. > Empirical results (especially on SMAC) are not strong enough in my opinion. The authors argue that "Many researchers in MARL regard the performance as the only standard to evaluate an algorithm, while we would argue that the interpretability is also significant, especially to the deployment in industry." While I certainly agree that the performance shouldn't be the only standard to evaluate an algorithm, I'd still expect the proposed method to be able to outperform all existing methods by a significant margin on at least one or two tasks, since in the two tested domains, I'm not very sure how useful the interpretability really is.

**Response**: We thank the reviewer for such an insightful comment. We understand the reviewer's thought standing by view of the most of MARL researchers in the community. In our view, this is an open question, but we are very happy to share our thoughts with the reviewer. We think the evaluation criterion is dependent on the purpose of a paper rather than the category of tasks. Please think about the following question. Why do the most of researchers test on environments such as SMAC? In our view, this is mainly because SMAC is complicated enough so that it can be selected as a candidate to abstract many real scenarios. The main purpose of AI/ML/RL is to deal with the real-world problem, which is also the purpose for Deepmind to study AlphaGo. The purpose of this paper follows a similar way, i.e., to solve a real-world problem, but demonstrate the perfomance on **a more familiar platform to the community**. This work only shows the possibility of interpretability of the proposed method, and then we plan to further study its interpretability on a specific application, i.e. electric power networks. In this real-world application, interpretability is important [2]. Why not choose a real-world task directly? In addition to the reason for familiarity to the community, there is another reason that the construction of a complicated real-world simulator is not easy. This naturally leads to a solution that is using game simulators as targets for demonstrating the performance of algorithms. This is also the roadmap of Deepmind. We are very happy to continue discussing this open question with the reviewer.


2. > The authors provide some discussion about the main differences between their work and [1] (at page 6). Algorithmically, it is clear that they propose a new multi-agent value-based method (SHAQ), while [1] proposes a multi-agent actor-critic method (SQDDPG). But they share the same key idea of using Shapley Q-values. Theoretically, it seems that the main difference is that the authors fixed a problem in [1] and then show that the generalised Shapley value is a solution in the $\epsilon^{*}$-core of Markov convex game. I might miss some other important theoretical contributions. Can the authors clarify this? Also, what are the practical differences between your theoretical results and the ones in [1]?

**Response**: We thank the reviewer for such an important concern. We now explain it in details. Actually, [1] firstly aligned the concepts of Markov convex game (MCG) to the global reward game, so that the value factorisation (assignment) looks more reasonable. However, the main problem for [1] is that the closed form of Shapley value for MCG is incorrect (though the approximation in [1] would not be impacted). In our work, we correct it and give a complete theoretical proof to make such a framework become more solid. This is **significant** to the further research following our work. On the other hand, constructing a learning process (say Q-learning) to find a solution is another contribution in this work that guides empirical learning algorithm called Shapley Q-learning with theoretical guarantees. We also construct an **empirical** model in Eq. (12)-(15), following the **distinct** theoretical results from [1] (i.e., Shapley-Q operator and the condition in Theorem 2).

As for "But they share the same key idea of using Shapley Q-values.", we would say Shapley (Q-)value is a general concept. Finding its correct closed-from expression is the significant theoretical contribution that the reviewer might miss. This directly supports the rationality of using the idea of Shapley (Q-)value in the MCG with the grand coalition (that is equivalent to the global reward game) rather than the intuition.

We wish our reply can remove the concerns from the reviewer.

content.title: Response to Reviewer mYrf (2/2)
content.comment:
3. > The predator-prey tasks chosen in the paper are for modelling relative overgeneralization. Why were these type of tasks chosen? Why are SHAQ and VDN better at tackling relative overgeneralization than other baseline methods? Actually, the term "relative overgeneralization" was never even mentioned before the experiment section about predator-prey. I think more discussion should be provided regarding this.

**Response**: First, this type of task is a common problem exists in MARL revealed by [3] and also used in [4]. In this work, we just use it as a testbed to evaluate algorithms like [4]. However, to let it more clear to all readers, we add the brief summary on this problem in the experiment section. As for the reason why SHAQ and VDN can well handle this problem, it is an interesting problem that deserves to be studied in the future though it is irrelevant to the main contributions of this work. We thank the reviwer for this interesting question.

4. > On predator-prey, why is SQDPPG not compared against (I couldn't find it in the appendix either)? Also, the authors mention that "W-QMIX does not perform as well as reported in Rashid et al. (2020). The reason could be its poor robustness to the increased explorations (Rashid et al., 2020) for this environment." How does W-QMIX perform with less exploration, say annealing $\epsilon$ over 10k/50k timesteps instead of 1mil?

**Response**: We have run the experiments that the reviewer would like shown in Figure 9 in the revised paper. Due to the burden resource consumption of SQDDPG, we only run it on p=-2. We would add the rest results for p=-1 and p=-0.5 later.

5. > If the generalized Shapley value can be thought of as a linear value factorization, I think it might be useful to discuss the limitations some, as I'd assume some tasks might need a non-linear value factorization to solve.

**Response**: We thank for the reviewer's suggestions. Although the reviewer's thought sounds reasonable, we would argue that non-linear factorization (such as QMIX) is difficult to analyze unless given the strong assumption such as IGM [5]. Moreover, linear decomposition of a problem is a common strategy for non-linear problem approximation [6] that also supports the idea of linear factorization for the global value under the context of MARL. The main limitation of linear value factorization is the loss of the accuracy of the approximation. Nonetheless, non-linear value factorization is still an open question deserves to be studied in the future. We wish our explanations can satisfy the reviewer. 

Finally, we wish our explanations can address the reviewer's concern and the decision can be reconsidered.


**Reference**

[1] Shapley q-value: A local reward approach to solve global reward games. Wang et al. AAAI 2020.

[2] Wang, Jianhong, et al. "Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Active Voltage Control on Power Distribution Networks." arXiv preprint arXiv:2110.14300 (2021).

[3] Wei, Ermo, and Sean Luke. "Lenient learning in independent-learner stochastic cooperative games." The Journal of Machine Learning Research 17.1 (2016): 2914-2955.

[4] Tabish Rashid, Gregory Farquhar, Bei Peng, and Shimon Whiteson.  Weighted qmix:  Expandingmonotonic value function factorisation for deep multi-agent reinforcement learning.Advances inNeural Information Processing Systems, 33, 2020.

[5] Son, Kyunghwan, et al. "Qtran: Learning to factorize with transformation for cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2019.

[6] Bertsimas, Dimitris, and John N. Tsitsiklis. Introduction to linear optimization. Vol. 6. Belmont, MA: Athena Scientific, 1997.

content.title: Re: Post Rebuttal
content.comment:
Thanks the reviewer for the post rebuttal comment, though it is so **hidden** (not let us know immediately by the normal forum response mode) and **late**. We now give further responses.

First, the significance of the theoretical results are not easily decided just as per the current popular topics. As we explained to the reviewer, interpretability for practical algorithms is important especially for the deployment on real-world applications, but it is unfortunately ignored. Our work builds upon [1] and gives a solid theoretical guarantees that was missing in [1], therefore we think our theoretical contribution is explicit. On the other hand, as the ICLR review code said "The research community is so big that somebody will find some value in the paper (maybe even a few years down the road), even if you don’t see it right now.", we don't agree this concern from the reviewer can be regarded as a criterion for rejecting a paper.

Second, for the practical differences, we uploaded the code to the supplementary materials and [1] also open source the code. We believe that if the reviewer can check it patiently, he/she will find that except for the collection of permutation of agents, the implementation of the learning process and the Shapley Q-value approximation in [1] and our paper are **completely** different. The illustrations on algorithm and implementations in both papers can also explicitly show the differences.

We wish our responses can address the reviewer's concerns.

replying_to: Replying to Re: Post Rebuttal
display_title: Further explanation for the practical differences between [1] and our work

content.title: Further explanation for the practical differences between [1] and our work
content.comment:
To further explain the practical differences between [1] and our work, we now specifically list the points as below:

* In [1], the Shapley Q-value is approximated by the average of the learned marginal contributions for sampled coalitions (so it is centralised), while in our work we directly approximate the Shapley Q-value as a local Q-value **thanks to** our theoretical results so that it can be used in Q-learning framework with decentralised control.
* The loss function for training Shapley-Q value in [1] is similar to VDN (see Eq. 11 in [1]), while **thanks to** our theoretical results our loss function is so **different** from [1] (see Eq. 14 in our paper) since there is additional $\hat{\delta}\_{i} ( \mathbf{s}, a\_{i}; \lambda)$ that does not appear in [1]. Meanwhile, we stated in Related Work that VDN is actually a special case of our proposed loss function in Eq. 14.
* The construction of $\hat{\alpha}\_{i}(\mathbf{s}, a\_{i})$ within $\hat{\delta}\_{i} (\mathbf{s}, a\_{i}; \lambda)$ in our work was **obviously** never mentioned in the practical implementation in [1].

Therefore, we definitely believe and confirm that **the practical implemetation in [1] and our work are completely different**.

We wish the reviewer can check it again and give a fair evaluation.

display_title: Official Review of Paper548 by Reviewer t47P

content.summary_of_the_paper:
If I understand correctly, this paper uses Shapley value as weights to improve learning in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems.  The technique is demonstrated in two [symmetric?] environments - a predator-prey problem, and a Starcraft problem - achieving good performance in both.

I found the exposition hindered my understanding of the paper, making it difficult both to understand the paper's contributions, and their correctness.
content.main_review:
**Strengths**

Clearly, training RL agents is an important problem - and has served as the foundation of some significant developments in ML (q.v. DeepMind's work).  Further, the manuscript seems to validate its approach by showing good performance in two environments.

Finally, the authors seem to have a strong grasp of the literature.

**Weaknesses**

Below, I score the manuscript as a "3 - reject", and my confidence as a "2".  A large part of my lack of confidence owes to the paper's exposition, which I found poor - making it hard for me to understand what the paper is doing.  If I had difficulty with it, as someone with knowledge of both RL and game theory, I am confident that other readers will as well.  I think that it would be difficult to conduct and review a thorough rewrite of the paper during the review period.

I would therefore suggest:
1. rewrite for English quality.  At present, a lot of the English is confusing or imprecise.
1. do less, better.  A whole jumble of techniques are deployed, often without being properly introduced: e.g. p.1 talks about cooperative, non-cooperative and coalitional game theory, without explaining the roles that each of these play in the paper - or seeming to recognize that 'cooperative' and 'coalitional' are synonyms when describing classes of games.  This continues.  For example:
    1. rather than introducing the necessary game theory at the start of Section 2, we launch straight into Markov convex games - without knowing what makes them Markovian or convex.
    1. Q-values are "defined" by presenting ranges of possible values, rather than actual definitions
    1. a "condition for MCG" is presented, without us being told what sort of condition it is: necessary or sufficient, and to what end (e.g. do equations of this form characterize MCGs? is this some sort of supermodularity condition?)
    1. the "value assignment", $\\bf{x}$, appears without explanation
    1. the core is defined verbally
    1. "rationality" is used without appearing to have any precise definition
    1. I would probably avoid the term "generalized Shapley value", which is already used - in a different sense - by Marichal and co-authors.
    1. what does $\mathcal{C}_i \cup \\{ i \\}$ mean?  Relatedly, what are "independent" policies?
    1. the $\sim$ in $C_i \sim p(C_i | N \backslash \\{i\\})$ suggests a distribution, which does not make sense in the context given.  What is this?
    1. I think that "almost no agents" (p.4) actually means "no agent has a large incentive"
    1. things like $\\bf{w}$ (presumably weights?) should be properly explained, and motivated
    1. any claim of "apparent" or "obviously" should be reflected upon: is it?
    1. what is the "history of each agent" in a Markovian game?
    1. statements like "a solution in the core of MCG with the grand coalition" are a bit confusing: there is a MCG; a certain value will arise from the grand coalition; I'm not sure what the phrase as a whole means.
    1. etc.

In conclusion, proper intuitions need to be supplied throughout: what are you doing, and why?  Why do the results derived make sense?
content.summary_of_the_review: I believe that the authors likely know what they are doing, but have not yet communicated it clearly enough for a reader to easily understand what they are doing.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.confidence: 2: You are willing to defend your assessment, but it is quite likely that you did not understand the central parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper548 by Reviewer t47P

content.title: Response to Reviewer t47P (1/2)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the detailed and thoughtful comments. We will try our best to address the concerns from the reviewer.

1. > rather than introducing the necessary game theory at the start of Section 2, we launch straight into Markov convex games - without knowing what makes them Markovian or convex.

**Response**: Markovian is the plug-in of the dynamics $p( \mathbf{s}' | \mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a} )$. The convexity is defined by Eq. (1) that is consistent to the Shapley's definition for the original convex game [1].

2. > Q-values are "defined" by presenting ranges of possible values, rather than actual definitions.

**Response**: To our best knowledge, Q-value is an approximation of cumulative (discounted) rewards that has no exact form [2, 3]. What does the reviewer mean by the actual definitions? Is that the form such as $Q^{\pi}: \mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{A} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$? 

3. > a "condition for MCG" is presented, without us being told what sort of condition it is: necessary or sufficient, and to what end (e.g. do equations of this form characterize MCGs? is this some sort of supermodularity condition?)

**Response**: It is a condition that characterize MCGs. As we check the term on Wikipedia [4], we would say it is equivalent to supermoduarity condition. However, as the references shown in [4], the name of supermodularity should come after the name of convex game [1] and from a different background. All terminologies in our work follow the work from convex game. We have commented this in the revised paper. Thanks for the reviewer's suggestion. 

4. > the "value assignment", $\mathbf{x}$, appears without explanation

**Response**: Value assignment (Credit assignment) is a common terminology in the context of MARL that means assigning the proper value to each agent. $\mathbf{x}$ is explained in the paper that is value assignment schemes, i.e., "The solution of MCG is a tuple containing a collection of coalitions called coalition structure and a value assignment scheme to agents under different coalitions. Mathematically, this tuple is represented as $\langle \mathcal{CS}, \mathbf{x}(\mathbf{s}) \rangle$, where $\mathcal{CS}=\{\mathcal{C}\_{1}, ..., \mathcal{C}\_{n}\}$ and $\mathbf{x}(\mathbf{s})=\langle x\_{i}(\mathbf{s}) \rangle_{i \in \mathcal{N}}, \forall \mathbf{s} \in \mathcal{S}$." We have described it more explicitly in the revised paper.

5. > the core is defined verbally

**Response**: The definition of core is just setting $\epsilon=0$. Due to the page limit, it is difficult to rewrite the definition of core in detail in the main part of paper. We wish the reviewer can sympathize this situation.

6. > "rationality" is used without appearing to have any precise definition

**Response**: The rationality is defined as the solution in the ($\epsilon$-)core, which is also consistent with the original definition in the coorperative game theory. We mentioned it in the first paragraph of Section 3, i.e., "show that the generalised Shapley value lies in the $\epsilon^{*}$-core of MCG with the grand coalition (i.e., rationality)". We have expressed it more clearly in the revised paper in the definition of MCG.

7. > I would probably avoid the term "generalized Shapley value", which is already used - in a different sense - by Marichal and co-authors.

**Response**: Thanks for the reviewer's suggestion. However, we cannot find a better name at present. In our view, it is not a critical problem, just like there are plenty of fixed point theorems. If the reviewer has some good name, we are happy to take a listen.

8. > what does $\mathcal{C}_{i} \cup \{i\}$ mean? Relatedly, what are "independent" policies?

**Response**: First, $\mathcal{C}\_{i}$ means a coalition of agents precedes agent $i$ during the process of constructing a grand coalition. Accordingly, $\mathcal{C}\_{i} \cup \{i\}$ means the coalition including both agents belonging to $\mathcal{C}\_{i}$ and agent $i$. Independent policies mean the joint policy indepdently decomposed, e.g., $\pi\_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{C}} = \times\_{i \in \mathcal{C}} \pi\_{i}, \forall \mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{N}$. We would mention these in the revised paper.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer t47P (1/2)

content.title: Response to Reviewer t47P (2/2)
content.comment:
9. > the $\sim$ in $C_{i} \sim p(\mathcal{C}_{i} | \mathcal{N} \backslash \\{i\\})$ suggests a distribution, which does not make sense in the context given. What is this?

**Response**: As we mentioned in the paper, "$\frac{|\mathcal{C}\_{i}|!(|\mathcal{N}|-|\mathcal{C}\_{i}|-1)!}{|\mathcal{N}|!}$ can be seen as the probability measure over $\mathcal{C}\_{i}$, i.e., $\mathit{p}(\mathcal{C}\_{i} | \mathcal{N} \backslash \\{i\\})$". In other words, $\mathit{p}(\mathcal{C}\_{i} | \mathcal{N} \backslash \\{i\\}) = \frac{|\mathcal{C}\_{i}|!(|\mathcal{N}|-|\mathcal{C}\_{i}|-1)!}{|\mathcal{N}|!}$ can be seen as the occurrence frequency of each $\mathcal{C}_{i}$ appearing during all possibilities of forming a grand coalition. This is actually a common sense in the cooperative game theory. We also provide a comment on the implementaion of sampling $\mathcal{C}\_{i}$ in Appendix C to help the audience understand it.

10. > I think that "almost no agents" (p.4) actually means "no agent has a large incentive"

**Response**: Yes, we agree with the reviewer's viewpoint. The reviewer's statement is an equivalent expression to ours.

11. > things like $\mathbf{w}$ (presumably weights?) should be properly explained, and motivated

**Response**: We thank the reviewer for bringing this concern. $\mathbf{w}$ is actually a transformation parameter that exists in fact. We agree that it is better give an explanation on this, however, this is difficult to be done for now. We are happy to investigate it in the future work.

12. > any claim of "apparent" or "obviously" should be reflected upon: is it?

**Response**: Thanks for the reviewer's suggestion. We would check every such word. However, it is better the reviewer can point out the specific positions for the inappropriate use of these words. For now, most of such words we use in the paper is for the trivial results that the readers can easily observe.

13. > what is the "history of each agent" in a Markovian game?

**Response**: "history of each agent" is actually the history of states and actions used for learning (or detecting) the actual state of a Markov game  with the global reward, i.e., analogous to the use of Kalman filter. We use this term since in actual experiments, each agent receives a partial observation (that is common in MARL) so that it forms a Dec-POMDP [5] that can be regarded as Markov game with partial observations. If the state filter (or detector) is (presumably) strong enough, then Dec-POMDP can be reduced to a Markov game with the global reward that matches the theoretical results in the paper. We wish our explanation can address the reviewer's concerns.

14. > statements like "a solution in the core of MCG with the grand coalition" are a bit confusing: there is a MCG; a certain value will arise from the grand coalition; I'm not sure what the phrase as a whole means.

**Response**: If we understand correctly, the reviewer may be confused of the concept of solution. First, there exists a value called global value representing the payoff (or utility) of the grand coalition. The solution here means finding a sort of value factorisation (decomposition) scheme to factorise the global value so that the condition of ($\epsilon$-)core is satisfied. The generalised Shapley value is such a kind of value factorisation method, i.e., a solution in the core of MCG with the grand coalition. We wish our explanation can remove the confusion of the reviewer.

Finally, we wish the reviewer's concerns can be addressed after our explanations and the decision can be reconsidered.

**Reference**

[1] Lloyd S Shapley. Cores of convex games.International journal of game theory, 1(1):11–26, 1971.

[2] Sutton, Richard S., and Andrew G. Barto. Reinforcement learning: An introduction. MIT press, 2018.

[3] Bertsekas, Dimitri. Reinforcement learning and optimal control. Athena Scientific, 2019.

[4] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supermodular_function

[5] Oliehoek, Frans A. "Decentralized pomdps." Reinforcement Learning. Springer, Berlin, Heidelberg, 2012. 471-503.

display_title: thank you for clearly indicating revisions in blue: my overall assessment remains that this paper needs to be written more clearly for a large audience

content.title: thank you for clearly indicating revisions in blue: my overall assessment remains that this paper needs to be written more clearly for a large audience
content.comment:
My initial review centered on my difficulties understanding this paper, in spite of familiarity with both RL and cooperative game theory.  I felt that a thorough rewrite was required, but would be difficult to achieve in the short revision period.

I am grateful to the authors for clearly indicating their revisions in blue.  These make clear that the revised paper has largely chosen not to address my concerns.  It _may_ be that readers more expert than I can pick out value that I cannot detect.  If that is the path that the authors wish to pursue, I would recommend submission to a more specialist venue.

On a number of points, the authors' replies to my concerns seemed confused:
- (#11) they propose to explain and motivate $\mathbf{w}$ in "future work".  This does not help readers of this paper.
- (#10) the authors believe that there claim that "almost no agents" is equivalent to "no agents have a large incentive" seems very incorrect: the former means refers to very few agents, but says nothing about the incentives that they face; the latter refers to all agents, but bounds incentives.  In _expected_ terms, they may be equivalent, but - if that is what is meant - it should be clearer.
- (#6) I remain confused by the authors' use of rationality.  In response to iyEm, they claim that the "(epsilon-)core concept is a solution concept that is a condition for defining rationality by the viewpoint of cooperative game theory".  This seems backwards: rationality is typically a primitive, a set of axioms (e.g. completeness and transitivity of a binary order),thus defining legitimate logical operations; similarly, a solution concept is also typically a primitive.  In non-cooperative game theory, a rational agent may backward induct to form a subgame perfect equilibrium: it would be meaningless to claim that a subgame equilibrium defines the agent's reasoning.  The paper's Conclusion claims that the authors have proved something about rationality: given the basic confusions here (e.g. purely verbal definitions, seemingly confused logic), I cannot understand what this means.

In conclusion, I am afraid that the authors' replies do not lead me to alter my assessment.  If they are unsuccessful publishing the paper as it stands at ICLR, I again recommend that they thoroughly rewrite it, taking proper exposition much more seriously.

replying_to: Replying to thank you for clearly indicating revisions in blue: my overall assessment remains that this paper needs to be written more clearly for a large audience

content.title: Further Response to Reviewer t47P
content.comment:
1. > (#11) they propose to explain and motivate in "future work". This does not help readers of this paper.

**Response**: We would emphasize that **not** every component in a work can have its explanations at the beginning. The explanation of this $w$ is not the key factor to understand our work. Besides, it is unfair to neglect the rest of contributions on MARL and the derived algorithm just because of this weakness. Finally, we believe that a work or subject should progress step by step and our work provides a foundation for the further work.

2. > (#10) the authors believe that there claim that "almost no agents" is equivalent to "no agents have a large incentive" seems very incorrect: the former means refers to very few agents, but says nothing about the incentives that they face; the latter refers to all agents, but bounds incentives. In expected terms, they may be equivalent, but - if that is what is meant - it should be clearer.

**Response**: For this point, we would argue that this is due to the different phrases, and we have the same idea as the reviewer's understanding. Additionally, we would add one point that we e missed in the last answer to this question that in the original version of paper we used "almost no agents tend", but the reviewer may miss the important word "tend". Therefore, we don't agree with the reviewer's words such as "seems very incorrect". Nevertheless, we agree that the reviewer's phrase could be more accurate and clearer, so we have changed it in the latest revised version of paper. 

3. > (#6) I remain confused by the authors' use of rationality. In response to iyEm, they claim that the "(epsilon-)core concept is a solution concept that is a condition for defining rationality by the viewpoint of cooperative game theory". This seems backwards: rationality is typically a primitive, a set of axioms (e.g. completeness and transitivity of a binary order),thus defining legitimate logical operations; similarly, a solution concept is also typically a primitive. In non-cooperative game theory, a rational agent may backward induct to form a subgame perfect equilibrium: it would be meaningless to claim that a subgame equilibrium defines the agent's reasoning. The paper's Conclusion claims that the authors have proved something about rationality: given the basic confusions here (e.g. purely verbal definitions, seemingly confused logic), I cannot understand what this means.

**Response**: We thank the reviewer for sharing his/her understanding on the rationality. The definition of (epsilon-)core is a solution concept that usually is thought to capture the notion of rationality [1, Page 5]. The original solution concept of (epsilon-)core is defined by Shapley [2] and we extend it to the scenario with state space and action space. This is a natural extension that is analogous to extend Nash equilibrium for static scenario to (stationary) Markov (perfect) equilibrium for dynamic scenario where dynamics are governed by Markov process [3]. "Equivalently, we can define a subgame perfect equilibrium to be a strategy profile $s^{\*}$ in  for which for any history h the strategy profile $s^{\*}|h$ is a Nash equilibrium of the subgame (h)." [4, Page 97] Accordingly, if Nash equilibrium (well known) can define the rationality, then of course subgame (perfect) equilibrium can, so as Markov (perfect) equilibrium and $epsilon-$core defined in our paper. In the context of game theory, the solution concept plays the role of a rational evaluation criterion that guides agents to find the solution (or reason). The reviewer's attitude on struggling on the solution concept is respected, however, we would argue that the solution concept here is just a primitive for the validity of importing Shapley value. The rest of works on finding the optimal Shapley value and demonstrating the interpretability in implementation are more critical. 

We are very pleased to discuss with the reviewer.




**Reference**

[1] "A key concern in game theory is to try to understand what counts as a rational outcome of a game. To this end, game theorists have developed a number of solution concepts, which for every game identify some subset of the possible outcomes of the game. If we think of a solution concept as capturing some notion of rationality, then the outcomes of a game identified in this way will represent the rational outcomes of the game." in Chalkiadakis, Georgios, Edith Elkind, and Michael Wooldridge. "Computational aspects of cooperative game theory." Synthesis Lectures on Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning 5.6 (2011): 1-168.

[2] Lloyd S Shapley. Cores of convex games.International journal of game theory, 1(1):11–26, 1971.

[3] He, Wei, and Yeneng Sun. "Stationary Markov perfect equilibria in discounted stochastic games." Journal of Economic Theory 169 (2017): 35-61.

[4] Osborne, Martin J., and Ariel Rubinstein. A course in game theory. MIT press, 1994.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the theoretical framework for value factorisation in multi-agent RL, with interpretability, under the framework of Markov convex games.
content.main_review:
The paper is generally well-written, including some interesting ideas. However, the current form seems still need some modification before it is ready to be accepted. Moreover, I am a bit concerned about the generality of the results (due to the assumption on MCG) on general MARL, and the disconnection between the theory and the experiments. The theoretical results seem interesting, but not strong enough (Especially given the existing results in Wang et al., 2020c). I would then view the contribution of the paper mainly on the empirical side. I will leave it to other reviewers and the AC who are more qualified than me to evaluate the empirical significance of the work. Please see my other comments as follows:

1. Some acronyms, e.g., MCG and SHAQ, has been defined multiple times. Please check all.
2. What is the implication of Eq. (2), i.e., the definition of the MCG? It would be better if the authors could provide more justifications for the generality and usefulness of the model, e.g., by examples.
3. Following 2, how the techniques in the current paper might be extended to the Markov games without the convexity structure?
4. When citing equations, there should be parentheses. 
5. Some notations may need more explanation: what is $R$ in Eq. (7)? What does the $\phi$ in the subscript of the definition in Eq. (5) and (6) mean? What is the definition of $w_i$ in Eq. (7), for those a that is not argmax?
6. Why after Eq. (7), $Q_i^{\phi*}$ can be written as linear function of $w_i$?
7. Related to 5, how should one set $w_i$, and how restricted the condition in Theorem 2 is? 
8. For the simulations, do we know if the environments are MCGs? In other words, do they satisfy the convexity condition in the definition? If not, it might not be fair to say that the experiments "verifies the theoretical results ".

content.title: Response to Reviewer VzRQ (1/2)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful comments. We will try our best to address the concerns from the reviewer.

1. > The theoretical results seem interesting, but not strong enough (Especially given the existing results in Wang et al., 2020c).

**Response**: As for whether the theoretical results are strong or not, we may have a different idea. Actually, Wang et al., 2020c firstly aligned the concepts of Markov convex game (MCG) to the global reward game, so that the value factorisation (assignment) looks more reasonable. However, the main problem for Wang et al., 2020c is that the closed form of Shapley value for MCG is incorrect (though the approximation in Wang et al., 2020c would not be impacted). In our work, we correct it and give a complete theoretical proof to make such a framework become more solid. This is beneficial for the further research following this track. On the other hand, constructing a learning process (say Q-learning) to find a solution is another contribution in this work, while Wang et al., 2020c mainly showed the existence of such a solution. Thrid, in our work we also empirically modelled such an operator to form a learning algorithm (Shapley Q-learning) guided by our theoretical results and verified the theoretical analysis. We wish the reviewer can recognise our theoretical results after our explanations.

2. > Some acronyms, e.g., MCG and SHAQ, has been defined multiple times. Please check all.

**Response**: Thanks for the reviewer's catch. We originally thought this could be convenient for the readers. If it is not, we will remove the rest of definitions in the next version of paper. 

3. > What is the implication of Eq. (2), i.e., the definition of the MCG? It would be better if the authors could provide more justifications for the generality and usefulness of the model, e.g., by examples.

**Response**: Thanks for the reviewer's good point. We completely agree with this point. Therefore, we actually have given more illustrations in the section Additional Background in Appendix A.2. We wish the reviewer can check it.

4. > Following 2, how the techniques in the current paper might be extended to the Markov games without the convexity structure?

**Response**: This is a pretty good question. In our work, the convexity structure is a promising way for defining and explaining value factorisation within the global reward game. Without the convexity structure, we may need to consider the coalition structure, i.e., forming groups and considering the value factorisation within each group. This is also a cutting-edge problem in the community of MARL. We think this could be an evidence to show the value of our work. We are happy to keep discussing this question with the reviewer.

5. > When citing equations, there should be parentheses.

**Response**: Thanks for the reviewer's suggestion. Unfortunately, the default \eqref command provided by ICLR format is also without parentheses. So, we think both styles could be acceptable.

6. > Some notations may need more explanation: what is $R$ in Eq. (7)? What does the $\phi$ in the subscript of the definition in Eq. (5) and (6) mean? What is the definition of $w_{i}$ in Eq. (7), for those a that is not argmax?

**Response**: $R$ in Eq. (7) is the global reward and we now define it in the Background in the revised paper. The $\phi$ in the superscript in Eq. (5) and (6) means the definition of Shapley value and Shapley Q-value. $w_{i}$ in Eq. (7) for those a that is not argmax, is actually a value that we need to find. This is the reason why we need to learn $\delta_{i}(\mathbf{s}, a_{i})$ defined in Eq. (10) so that the $w_{i}$ in Eq. (7) for those a that is not argmax can be found that also makes the condition in Theorem 2 hold. We wish these explanations can remove the concerns from the reviewer.

7. > Why after Eq. (7), $Q_{i}^{\phi^{*}}$ can be written as linear function of $w_{i}$?

**Response**: If we understand the reviewer's point correctly, the reviewer may misunderstand the logic of statement here. The $Q^{ \phi^{*} }_{i} ( \mathbf{s}, a\_{i} ) = w\_{i} ( \mathbf{s}, a\_{i} ) \ Q^{\pi}\_{\*} ( \mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a} )$ under Eq. (7) is a suppose to reach Eq. (7).

8. > Related to 5, how should one set $w_{i}$, and how restricted the condition in Theorem 2 is?

**Response**: This is a good question. First, $\delta_{i}(\mathbf{s}, a_{i})$ in Eq. (10) for Shapley Q-learning includes $w_{i}$. In Eq. (12) and (13), we construct a model that is proven to make the condition in Theorem 2 hold (see Appendix B.5), which is actually mentioned in the paragraph below Eq. (13) in the paper. We wish the reviewer can check it again.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers a theoretical analysis of the value factorization problem in multi-agent reinforcement learning. To achieve this, they introduce a number of concepts: convex markov games, approximate core, coalition marginal contribution. They show that generalized shapley value lies in the approximate core of the convex markov game. They then prove rationality (among other properties) of generalized shapley value. Based on this, they derive shapley Q-learning which is a generalization of the bellman operation. They evaluate this algorithm on two datasets: Predator-Prey and multi-agent starcraft
content.main_review:
Strengths of this paper

+ Introduces a number of novel concepts and definition to theoretically explain the value factorization.
+ Based on theory, they also derive a new operator and algorithm which empirically performs well on challenging datasets
+ Comparison against pretty strong baselines: unlike many works in RL, they have done an pretty thorough job. 


Weakness of this paper

- First, I found this paper a bit hard to follow. Overall, it took me quite a bit of time to understand how the various concepts introduced are related. I propose the authors significantly rewrite the paper explaining how the various concepts relate. For instance, the core concept here is generalized shapley value having rationality and fairness properties which leads to the shapley Q-learning algorithm. The notion of convex markov games and core etc are just a means to an end. Yet the first technical parts directly talk about these notions which seems like a distraction.
- Second, looking at the experimental results, most of the CIs overlap. So in that sense, what is the main message of shapley Q-learning algorithm? Its not clear that it is strictly a better algorithm. Is the main takeaway that it can do as well as these other algorithms and also has strong theory for analyzing value decomposition? This relates to the first point above, the paper does not do a good job of connecting the various parts and giving a crisp takeaway.
content.summary_of_the_review: As above, most of my comments are around the presentation. This is related since I did not get a complete understanding of the main contributions of this papers; most importantly their significance. Addressing some of my suggestions above will definitely make this paper readable.

content.title: Response to Reviewer iyEm (1/2)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments. Then, we will try our best to address the concerns from the reviewer.

1. > First, I found this paper a bit hard to follow. Overall, it took me quite a bit of time to understand how the various concepts introduced are related. I propose the authors significantly rewrite the paper explaining how the various concepts relate. For instance, the core concept here is generalized shapley value having rationality and fairness properties which leads to the shapley Q-learning algorithm. The notion of convex markov games and core etc are just a means to an end. Yet the first technical parts directly talk about these notions which seems like a distraction.

**Response**: First, we well understand the situation that the reviewer meet when reading the paper. Actually, this is most probable due to the reason that the unfamilarity of cooperative game theory [1]. The concepts that the reviewer mentioned are actually common in the context of cooperative game theory. The reviewer can think of a question: many recent multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms claim that they are finding the solution called Nash equilibrium, however, have they explained these concepts? Most of them just gave a definition as we did in the paper. Due to the page limit, we have tried our best to illustrate these concepts in the most concise way, to make the most of audience get into the work as fast as possible. Also, we give additional background to introduce the concepts in Appendix. We wish the reviewer can check that. However, we still keep open to discuss with the reviewer about how to make it more friendly to most of readers. 

The ($\epsilon$-)core concept is a solution concept that is a condition for defining rationality by the viewpoint of cooperative game theory [1], analogous to Nash equilibrium in the non-cooperative game theory. We generalise it to the scenario with Markov dynacmics. (1) Markov convex game is a sort of game model, where the generalised Shapley value with a grand coalition is a valid solution to make the condition of ($\epsilon$-)core hold. (2) The property of fairness is a property of generalised Shapley value (as Definition 2 states). The combination of (1) and (2) leads to the rationality and fairness. Due to the equivalence of Markov convex game with a grand coalition and the global reward game, we can apply generalised Shapley value as a value factorisation method in the global reward game, to make it more reasonable than the prior works that directly assumed that the value can be factorised but with no reasons or intuitions (e.g. QMIX[2], VDN[3], etc.) and a stronger assumption called IGM to promise the convergence. The theory of Shapley value can be regarded as a method that fills the gap for IGM about the rationality of decomposition of maximum global value. **Therefore**, the notion of Markov convex games and core etc are not a means to an end, but the fundation of the application of Shapley value in the global reward game and multi-agent Q-learning. 

As for the reviewers' statement *"Yet the first technical parts directly talk about these notions which seems like a distraction."*, in our view it depends on the audience of the paper. Some readers may favour the definition written first in the technical part, but some others may like illustrating the intuition first. We actually put the motivation and the general overview of our contributions in the section Introduction, which is the manner that is possibly good in our view. Anyway, we still keep open to discuss with the reviewer about this question.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer iyEm (1/2)

content.title: Response to Reviewer iyEm (2/2)
content.comment:
2. > Second, looking at the experimental results, most of the CIs overlap. So in that sense, what is the main message of shapley Q-learning algorithm? Its not clear that it is strictly a better algorithm. Is the main takeaway that it can do as well as these other algorithms and also has strong theory for analyzing value decomposition? This relates to the first point above, the paper does not do a good job of connecting the various parts and giving a crisp takeaway.

**Response**: First, Shapley Q-learning can generally work well in various experiments as our experiments show. Second, the empirical performance and construction of models can validate our theoretical analysis, as well as its hyperparameters can be selected according to the an empirical laws as we demonmstrated in Appendix that is far better than W-QMIX [4] that needs manually selection of hyperparameters with no laws. We wish the reviewer can check experimental parts and Appendix again. Thrid, Shapley Q-learning possesses the interpretability of value factorisation that is lacking in the prior algorithms. In one word, the main message of Shapley Q-learning is that **it can not only possess a generally good performance, but also interpretability with a theoretical guarantee**. We conclude these in the section Conclusion. 

As for the defnition for the strictly better algorithm, we think that this is an open question especially in the current state of MARL/RL. As the recent work published on NeurIPS 2021 [5] shows, the interpretability is also critical in the real-world application. We are happy to further discuss this question with the reviewer. Interpretability is a difficult problem for ML/RL, our paper is an attempt standing by the view of Shapley value theory to design a multi-agent Q-learning algorithm with interpretability.

Finally, we sincerely wish the reviewer can reconsider the decision, after reading our response. We are happy to have a further dicussion so that the reviewer and us can reach a concensus.


**Reference**

[1] Georgios Chalkiadakis, Edith Elkind, and Michael Wooldridge. Computational aspects of cooperativegame theory. Synthesis Lectures on Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, 5(6):1–168,2011.

[2] Tabish Rashid, Mikayel Samvelyan, Christian Schr ̈oder de Witt, Gregory Farquhar, Jakob N. Foerster,and Shimon Whiteson. QMIX: monotonic value function factorisation for deep multi-agentreinforcement learning. InProceedings of the 35th International Conference on Machine Learning,ICML 2018, Stockholmsm ̈assan, Stockholm, Sweden, July 10-15, 2018, volume 80 of Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, pp. 4292–4301. PMLR, 2018.

[3] Sunehag, Peter, et al. "Value-decomposition networks for cooperative multi-agent learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:1706.05296 (2017).

[4] Tabish Rashid, Gregory Farquhar, Bei Peng, and Shimon Whiteson.  Weighted qmix:  Expandingmonotonic value function factorisation for deep multi-agent reinforcement learning.Advances inNeural Information Processing Systems, 33, 2020.

[5] Wang, Jianhong, et al. "Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Active Voltage Control on Power Distribution Networks." arXiv preprint arXiv:2110.14300 (2021).
